The hypothesis says that f has a zero of order k at a, so write
f(z)=(z−a)kg(z),g(a)=0,
(15)
with g holomorphic near a. Differentiating gives
f′(z)=(z−a)k−1(kg(z)+(z−a)g′(z)).
(16)
Choose δ>0 so small that the closed disc D(a,δ) lies in the domain, g never vanishes there, and the parenthesized factor never vanishes there. Thus a is the only critical point of f in that disc.
On the boundary circle, f is nonzero. Set
ε=min∣z−a∣=δ​∣f(z)∣>0.
(17)
If 0<∣b∣<ε, then ∣b∣<∣f(z)∣ on the boundary. Rouché's theorem applied to f and f−b says that f−b has the same number of zeros in D(a,δ) as f, namely k, counted with multiplicity.
None of these zeros is a because b=0, and none is a critical point because f′ has no other zero in the disc. Every zero of f−b is therefore simple. Hence there are exactly
k distinct z∈D(a,δ) with f(z)=b​.

The one-dimensional Time-dependent Schrodinger equation for a wavefunction in a real potential is
iℏ∂t∂Ψ​=−2mℏ2​∂x2∂2Ψ​+UΨ.
(19)
Multiplying this equation by Ψ∗, multiplying its complex conjugate by Ψ, and subtracting gives the probability continuity equation
∂t∂∣Ψ∣2​+∂x∂j​=0,j=2miℏ​(Ψ∗∂x∂Ψ​−Ψ∂x∂Ψ∗​).
(20)
If Ψ and its first derivative decay sufficiently rapidly as x→±∞, then the probability current j vanishes at both ends. Integrating the continuity equation and using the fundamental theorem of calculus yields
dtd​∫−∞∞​∣Ψ(x,t)∣2dx=−j(∞,t)+j(−∞,t)=0.
(21)
This conservation of quantum probability is required by the Born rule: once a normalizable wavefunction has total probability one, its time evolution must preserve that normalization.
For the stated Gaussian wave packet, put β=ℏt/m. Since
f(t)=α+iβ1​,∣f(t)∣=α2+β2​1​,Ref(t)=α2+β2α​,
(22)
its squared modulus is

which is independent of time, as required.

For the simple random walk on the integer line, a return to the origin is possible only at an even time. At time 2n, exactly n of the increments must be +1, so the return probability is
p2n​=22n1​(n2n​).
(39)
The supplied factorial bounds, equivalently the order estimate in the Stirling formula, give
p2n​≍n−1/2.
(40)
Consequently ∑n​p2n​ diverges. By the recurrence criterion by return probabilities, the origin is a recurrent state; translation invariance then makes the whole walk recurrent.
For three independent walks, the probability that all three are at the origin at time 2n is
p2n3​=(4n(n2n​)​)3≍n−3/2.
(41)
This P-series is convergent, so the first of the Borel-Cantelli lemmas says that simultaneous returns occur only finitely often with probability one. Therefore the requested probability is
0​.

By the real spectral theorem, the real symmetric matrix A has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. In that basis the associated quadratic form is
q(x)=λ1​x12​+⋯+λn​xn2​.
(54)
Rescaling the coordinates belonging to nonzero eigenvalues changes every positive coefficient to +1 and every negative coefficient to −1. Hence the diagonal normal form has one positive square for each positive eigenvalue and one negative square for each negative eigenvalue. By Sylvester's law of inertia, these counts do not depend on the diagonalizing basis, so
signatureH=#{λi​>0}−#{λi​<0}​.
(55)
The numerical eigenvalues are not invariant under a general change of basis, because the matrix changes by congruence rather than similarity. For example, on a one-dimensional space let q(e)=1. Its matrix in the basis (e) is (1), whereas in the basis (2e) it is (4). The eigenvalue changes from 1 to 4, although its sign, and therefore the signature, is unchanged.

9G OurBigBook.com
For subgroups H,P≤G, define x∼y when y∈HxP. The identity elements show reflexivity, inverses show symmetry, and multiplication shows transitivity. Thus the double cosets HxP partition G.
Let H act by left multiplication on the set of left cosets G/P. The orbit of xP consists of the cosets contained in HxP, so its size is ∣HxP∣/∣P∣. Its stabilizer is
StabH​(xP)​={h∈H:hxP=xP}=H∩xPx−1.​
(56)
The orbit-stabilizer theorem therefore gives
∣P∣∣HxP∣​=∣H∩xPx−1∣∣H∣​​.
(57)
Suppose P is a Sylow subgroup of G, with ∣P∣=pa, and write the largest power of p dividing ∣H∣ as pb. If every H∩xPx−1 had order at most pb−1, the displayed formula would make every double-coset size divisible by pa+1. Their sum ∣G∣ would then also be divisible by pa+1, contradicting the choice of P. Hence some H∩xPx−1 has order pb and is a Sylow p-subgroup of H. This is the Sylow subgroup of a subgroup from double cosets argument.
To count the general linear group over a finite field GLn​(Fp​), choose its columns successively. There are pn−1 choices for the first, pn−p for the second, and pn−pk for column k+1. Consequently
∣GLn​(Fp​)∣=k=0∏n−1​(pn−pk)=pn(n−1)/2j=1∏n​(pj−1)​.
(58)
None of the factors pj−1 is divisible by p, so the upper unitriangular group is a Sylow p-subgroup: it has one arbitrary field entry in each of the n(n−1)/2 positions above the diagonal and hence order pn(n−1)/2. The permutation matrices form a subgroup isomorphic to the symmetric group Sn​.
By Cayley theorem, every finite group G embeds in S∣G∣​, and permutation matrices embed this symmetric group in GL∣G∣​(Fp​). The latter has the explicit Sylow p-subgroup just described, so the result proved in the first part, applied to the embedded copy of G, proves that every finite group has a Sylow p-subgroup.
The counting part of the Sylow theorems says that if pa is the largest power of p dividing ∣G∣, then the number np​ of Sylow p-subgroups satisfies
np​≡1(modp),np​∣∣G∣/pa​.
(59)
Finally, let ∣G∣=pq with prime numbers p>q. The Sylow counts give
np​∣q,np​≡1(modp),
(60)
so np​=1 and the Sylow p-subgroup is a normal subgroup. Also nq​∣p and nq​≡1(modq). If nq​=1, both Sylow subgroups are normal; their elements commute, so G is their direct product and is abelian. In the nonabelian case one must therefore have nq​=p, whence
p≡1(modq)​,
(61)
or equivalently q∣p−1, as recorded by nonabelian group of order pq.

hg(t,x+hei​)−g(t,x)​=∫01​Di​g(t,x+shei​)ds.
(62)
For sufficiently small h, the points (t,x+shei​) lie in a fixed compact set. The continuity of Di​g makes it uniformly continuous there, so the right-hand side converges to Di​g(t,x) uniformly in t. We may consequently pass the limit through the finite integral:
Di​G(x)​=h→0lim​∫01​hg(t,x+hei​)−g(t,x)​dt=∫01​Di​g(t,x)dt​.​
(63)
To prove continuity, if xk​→x, joint continuity makes Di​g(t,xk​)→Di​g(t,x) uniformly for t∈[0,1] once the xk​ lie in a compact neighbourhood of x. Hence Di​G(xk​)→Di​G(x). This proves the stated differentiation under the integral sign result and the continuity of every partial derivative.

11F OurBigBook.com
An abstract smooth surface is a Hausdorff second-countable topological space with an atlas of charts to open subsets of R2 whose transition maps are smooth. It is orientable when it has such an atlas for which every transition map has positive Jacobian determinant. A map f:S1​→S2​ is a smooth map when every coordinate representation
ψ∘f∘ϕ−1
(68)
is smooth wherever it is defined.
The map a:C→C is a smooth involution with no fixed point: the equation
(x,y,z)=(−x,−y,−z)
(69)
would force x=y=0, which is impossible on x2+y2=1. For each p∈C, choose a sufficiently small coordinate neighbourhood Up​ such that
Up​∩a(Up​)=∅.
(70)
Then the quotient projection restricts to a homeomorphism
π∣Up​​:Up​⟶π(Up​).
(71)
Transporting a smooth chart ϕp​:Up​→R2 across this homeomorphism gives the quotient chart
ϕ​p​=ϕp​∘(π∣Up​​)−1.
(72)
On an overlap, a lift lies either in another chosen neighbourhood or in its image under a. The corresponding transition map is therefore a transition map on C, possibly composed with the diffeomorphism a, and is smooth. Since this is a free action of the finite group {1,a}, the quotient is Hausdorff and second countable. This constructs the smooth quotient by a free finite group action, and in these charts π is locally the identity. Hence π is a local diffeomorphism, in particular smooth.
To test orientability, parametrize the cylinder by
F(θ,z)=(cosθ,sinθ,z).
(73)
The involution acts in these coordinates as
(θ,z)⟼(θ+π,−z),
(74)
whose derivative has determinant −1. Thus a is an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism of the cylinder.
If the quotient surface S were orientable, its orientation would pull back through the local diffeomorphism π to an orientation of C. The identity π∘a=π would then force a to preserve that pulled-back orientation, contradicting the negative determinant above. Therefore
S is not orientable​.
(75)

The Hamiltonian is the sum of three commuting one-dimensional harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonians. Its product eigenstates are
Ψnx​ny​nz​​(x,y,z)=ψnx​​(x)ψny​​(y)ψnz​​(z),
(113)
with energies
Enx​ny​nz​​=ℏω(nx​+ny​+nz​+23​)​.
(114)
Equivalently, the level with N=nx​+ny​+nz​ has energy EN​=ℏω(N+3/2), as in the three-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator.
Up to normalization, the ground-state wavefunction is
Ψ000​=exp[−2ℏMω​(x2+y2+z2)].
(115)
It is radial, so ∇Ψ000​ is parallel to the position vector. Since the orbital angular momentum is L=−iℏr×∇, every component of L annihilates this state. Therefore
Lz​Ψ000​=0,L2Ψ000​=0,
(116)
and the ground state has ℓ=m=0.
The first excited level has N=1 and is spanned by
xΨ000​,yΨ000​,zΨ000​.
(117)
The state
Φ0​=zΨ000​
(118)
satisfies Lz​Φ0​=0. Applying the ladder operators gives
L+​Φ0​=−ℏ(x+iy)Ψ000​,L−​Φ0​=ℏ(x−iy)Ψ000​.
(119)
Hence convenient m=±1 eigenstates are
Φ±1​=(x±iy)Ψ000​​,
(120)
up to normalization and irrelevant overall phases.
Finally, the isotropic Hamiltonian is rotationally invariant. The rotational invariance of a central-potential Hamiltonian gives
[H,Lz​]=[H,L2]=[Lz​,L2]=0.
(121)
These commuting self-adjoint operators can be simultaneously diagonalized within each energy eigenspace, which is why joint eigenstates of H,L2,Lz​ must exist.
